Write \(g_{t,a}(\theta)=g(a,X_t,Y_t(a);\theta)\). By the i.i.d.-full-data and sequential-randomization assumptions, and using uniform overlap to justify every inverse probability,
\[
\begin{aligned}
E_P[\xi_t\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]
&=E_P\!\left[E_P\!\left\{\left.\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}
 \frac{\mathbf 1\{A_t=a\}g_{t,a}(\theta^*)}
 {\pi_t(a\mid X_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})}\right|W_t,\mathcal F_{t-1}\right\}\middle|\mathcal F_{t-1}\right]\\
&=E_P\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}g_{t,a}(\theta^*)\right]
=M_P(\theta^*)=0.
\end{aligned} \tag{1}
\]
Thus \((\xi_t,\mathcal F_t)\) is a martingale-difference array. Define, only for this proof,
\[
 \Gamma_P(\eta)=E_P\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}
 \frac{g_{t,a}(\theta^*)g_{t,a}(\theta^*)^\top}
 {\Pi(a\mid X_t,\eta)}\right]. \tag{2}
\]
The same conditioning calculation as in (1) yields
\[
 E_P[\xi_t\xi_t^\top\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}]=\Gamma_P(\eta_{t-1}),
 \qquad \Omega_j=\Gamma_P(\bar\eta_j). \tag{3}
\]
The bounded-score and overlap assumptions imply \(\|\xi_t\|_2\le B/\varepsilon\). For every unit vector \(u\),
\[
 u^\top\Omega_ju
 \le E_P\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}
 \frac{\|g_{t,a}(\theta^*)\|_2^2}{\Pi(a\mid X_t,\bar\eta_j)}\right]
 \le \frac{KB^2}{\varepsilon}, \tag{4}
\]
which proves \(\Omega_j\preceq(KB^2/\varepsilon)I_d\). The derivative envelope permits differentiation through the finite sum and expectation, and therefore
\[
 \|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le E_P\!\left[\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}
 \|\partial_\theta g_{t,a}(\theta^*)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\right]
 \le KD_1. \tag{5}
\]

For \(p,q\ge\varepsilon\), \(|p^{-1}-q^{-1}|\le |p-q|/\varepsilon^2\). The policy-Lipschitz assumption and (2) consequently give
\[
 \|\Gamma_P(\eta)-\Gamma_P(\eta')\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le L_\Gamma\|\eta-\eta'\|_2,
 \qquad L_\Gamma=\frac{KB^2L_\Pi}{\varepsilon^2}, \tag{6}
\]
and \(\|\Gamma_P(\eta)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M_\Gamma:=KB^2/\varepsilon\). On
\[
 \mathcal A_T=\left\{T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T
 \|\eta_{t-1}-\bar\eta_J\|_2\le r_T\right\},
\]
equations (3) and (6) imply
\[
 \left\|T^{-1}\langle S\rangle_T-\Omega_J\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le L_\Gamma r_T. \tag{7}
\]
On \(\mathcal A_T^c\) the norm in (7) is at most \(2M_\Gamma\), while the uniform Cesaro-attraction assumption gives \(P(\mathcal A_T^c)\le\delta_T\). Hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}E_P\left\|T^{-1}\langle S\rangle_T-\Omega_J\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le L_\Gamma r_T+2M_\Gamma\delta_T
 \le C(r_T+\delta_T), \tag{8}
\]
for a constant depending only on the common envelopes.

We next derive localization. For fixed \(\theta\), sequential randomization and i.i.d. arrivals show that the summands of \(G_T(\theta)-M_P(\theta)\) are mean-zero martingale differences. Their Euclidean norms are uniformly bounded, so orthogonality of distinct martingale increments gives
\[
 E_P\|G_T(\theta)-M_P(\theta)\|_2^2\le C_0/T. \tag{9}
\]
The empirical and population maps are uniformly Lipschitz in \(\theta\), with respective moduli \(D_1/\varepsilon\) and \(KD_1\). For fixed \(x>0\), choose a finite mesh of the compact set \(\Theta\) fine enough that the two Lipschitz approximation errors sum to at most \(x/2\). Chebyshev's inequality applied to (9), followed by the union bound over this fixed mesh, proves
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P\left\{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}
 \|G_T(\theta)-M_P(\theta)\|_2>x\right\}\longrightarrow0. \tag{10}
\]
Since \(M_P(\theta^*)=0\) and the preliminary estimator satisfies its defining approximate-minimum inequality,
\[
 \|M_P(\widetilde\theta_T)\|_2
 \le2\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\|G_T(\theta)-M_P(\theta)\|_2
 +T^{-1/2}(r_T+\delta_T)=o_P(1) \tag{11}
\]
uniformly. The uniform-root-separation assumption now yields, for every \(u>0\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P\{\|\widetilde\theta_T-\theta^*\|_2\ge u\}
 \le\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P\{\|M_P(\widetilde\theta_T)\|_2\ge\kappa(u)\}
 \longrightarrow0. \tag{12}
\]

At \(\theta^*\), \(G_T(\theta^*)=S_T/T\), so (1), martingale orthogonality, and bounded increments imply \(G_T(\theta^*)=O_P(T^{-1/2})\) uniformly. Applying the same entrywise argument to the derivative score and using the derivative envelope gives
\[
 R_T:=\partial_\theta G_T(\theta^*)-H=O_P(T^{-1/2}) \tag{13}
\]
uniformly. On the closed \(\rho\)-ball about \(\theta^*\), the curvature and overlap bounds imply
\[
 \sup_{\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2\le\rho}
 \|\partial_\theta G_T(\theta)-H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le\|R_T\|_{\mathrm{op}}+D_2\rho/\varepsilon. \tag{14}
\]
The choice of \(\rho\), (13), and \(\sigma_{\min}(H)\ge h_-\) make the right-hand side smaller than \(h_-/2\) with probability tending uniformly to one. On that event define \(\Psi_T(\theta)=\theta-H^{-1}G_T(\theta)\). Equations (14) and \(\|H^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le h_-^{-1}\) show that \(\Psi_T\) has Lipschitz constant at most \(1/2\) on the ball. Moreover,
\[
 \|\Psi_T(\theta)-\theta^*\|_2
 \le\tfrac12\|\theta-\theta^*\|_2+h_-^{-1}\|G_T(\theta^*)\|_2. \tag{15}
\]
The last term is at most \(\rho/2\) with probability tending uniformly to one, and the root-interior assumption puts the closed ball inside \(\Theta\). Thus \(\Psi_T\) maps this complete closed ball into itself. Starting from any point in the ball, its iterates have successive distances bounded by a geometric sequence, hence are Cauchy; their limit \(\theta_T^0\) is a fixed point by continuity. If two fixed points existed, their distance would be at most half itself, so the fixed point is unique. Since fixed points are exactly roots,
\[
 \|\theta_T^0-\theta^*\|_2
 \le2h_-^{-1}\|G_T(\theta^*)\|_2=O_P(T^{-1/2}). \tag{16}
\]
Equations (12) and (16) imply that both \(\widetilde\theta_T\) and \(\theta_T^0\) are within \(\rho/4\) of \(\theta^*\) with probability tending uniformly to one. Then \(\theta_T^0\in\mathcal Z_T\), while every member of \(\mathcal Z_T\) is within \(3\rho/4\) of \(\theta^*\) and therefore equals the unique root \(\theta_T^0\) in the closed \(\rho\)-ball. Consequently
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P(E_T^c)\to0, \qquad
 \widehat\theta_T=\theta_T^0
\]
outside a uniformly negligible event.

Put \(\Delta_T=\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*\). On this exact-root event, Taylor's formula and the curvature bound give
\[
 0=G_T(\widehat\theta_T)
 =T^{-1}S_T+H\Delta_T+R_T\Delta_T+R_T^{(2)},
 \qquad
 \|R_T^{(2)}\|_2\le\frac{D_2}{2\varepsilon}\|\Delta_T\|_2^2. \tag{17}
\]
By (13) and (16), multiplication of (17) by \(\sqrt T H^{-1}\) proves
\[
 \sqrt T\Delta_T+H^{-1}T^{-1/2}S_T
 =O_P(T^{-1/2})=O_P(e_T). \tag{18}
\]
The fallback branch has probability tending uniformly to zero, so restoring it preserves this uniform-in-probability order.

It remains to establish the label-free distributional conclusion. Let
\[
 \beta_T=\max\{T^{-1/2},\sqrt{r_T}\},\qquad
 k_T=\lceil T\beta_T\rceil,\qquad
 \Lambda_T=k_T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^{k_T}\Gamma_P(\eta_{t-1}). \tag{19}
\]
The vanishing-modulus assumption gives \(k_T/T\to0\) and \(Tr_T/k_T\le\sqrt{r_T}+o(1)\). Since \(\Lambda_T\) is \(\mathcal F_{k_T}\)-measurable, the calculation leading to (8) gives
\[
 E_P\|\Lambda_T-\Omega_J\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le L_\Gamma\frac{Tr_T}{k_T}+2M_\Gamma\delta_T=o(1) \tag{20}
\]
uniformly. With
\[
 B_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T\Gamma_P(\eta_{t-1}),
\]
the same calculation, accounting for the omitted prefix, yields
\[
 E_P\|B_T-\Omega_J\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le L_\Gamma r_T+M_\Gamma k_T/T+2M_\Gamma\delta_T=o(1). \tag{21}
\]
Thus \(E_P\|B_T-\Lambda_T\|_{\mathrm{op}}=o(1)\) uniformly.

Fix a unit vector \(c\) and put \(a=H^{-\top}c\). Equations (5) and the Jacobian lower bound imply
\[
 (KD_1)^{-1}\le\|a\|_2\le h_-^{-1}. \tag{22}
\]
Therefore \(|a^\top\xi_t|\le B/(\varepsilon h_-)\), while regime nondegeneracy gives
\[
 a^\top\Omega_Ja\ge v_0:=\frac{\omega_-}{(KD_1)^2}>0. \tag{23}
\]
Also \(a^\top\Lambda_Ta\le v_+:=M_\Gamma/h_-^2\). The simultaneous bounds \(\omega_-I_d\preceq\Omega_j\preceq M_\Gamma I_d\) and \(h_-\le\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le KD_1\) imply \(v_0\le v_+\). Define the \(\mathcal F_{k_T}\)-measurable clipped variance
\[
 \lambda_{T,P,c}=\max\{v_0/2,a^\top\Lambda_Ta\}. \tag{24}
\]
Because (23) holds, (20)--(21) and \(\|a\|_2\le h_-^{-1}\) give
\[
 E_P|a^\top B_Ta-\lambda_{T,P,c}|=o(1) \tag{25}
\]
uniformly in \(P\) and unit \(c\). Apply \(\mathrm{lem:early\text{-}measurable\text{-}martingale\text{-}mixture}\) to \(X_{T,t}=-a^\top\xi_t\), \(\mathcal G_{T,t}=\mathcal F_t\), and (24). Its boundedness, positive lower variance, measurability, and quadratic-variation approximation hypotheses are respectively (22), (23)--(24), the definition in (19), and (25). Hence
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}
 \left|P\left\{-a^\top T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T\xi_t\le z\right\}
 -E_P\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{\lambda_{T,P,c}}}\right)\right|\to0. \tag{26}
\]
For variances in a fixed interval bounded away from zero, differentiation shows
\[
 \sup_z\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial v}\Phi(z/\sqrt v)\right|
 \le C/v.
\]
Equations (20) and (23)--(24) therefore permit replacement of the expectation in (26) by
\[
 E_P\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{a^\top\Omega_Ja}}\right)
 =\sum_{j\in\mathcal J_P}p_{P,j}\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{c^\top V_{P,j}c}}\right). \tag{27}
\]
Martingale orthogonality and bounded increments give
\[
 E_P\left|a^\top T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{k_T}\xi_t\right|^2
 \le Ck_T/T=o(1), \tag{28}
\]
so the prefix is uniformly negligible. The exact-root remainder in (18) is also uniformly \(o_P(1)\). The mixture distributions in (27) have densities uniformly bounded by the positive variance lower bound (23). For any \(\eta>0\), the elementary inclusions \(\{X+R\le z\}\subseteq\{X\le z+\eta\}\cup\{|R|>\eta\}\) and \(\{X\le z-\eta\}\subseteq\{X+R\le z\}\cup\{|R|>\eta\}\), followed first by \(T\to\infty\) and then \(\eta\downarrow0\), transfer (26)--(28) through both remainders. This proves the asserted uniform finite-mixture approximation.

The regime covariance matrices obey the common bounds
\[
 \frac{\omega_-}{(KD_1)^2}I_d\preceq V_{P,j}
 \preceq\frac{KB^2}{\varepsilon h_-^2}I_d. \tag{29}
\]
The upper bound uses (4) and \(\|H^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le h_-^{-1}\); the lower bound uses \(\Omega_j\succeq\omega_-I_d\) and (5). There are finitely many possible supports. Repeatedly select convergent subsequences of the finitely many bounded weights and matrix entries; (29) keeps every matrix limit positive definite. This produces the subsequence and limits stated in the theorem. The uniform CDF approximation then gives its centered Gaussian-mixture limit, with zero limiting weights omitted.

If \(q_j=c^\top V_j^\infty c\) and \(\bar q=\sum_jp_j^\infty q_j\), the second and fourth moments of the limiting finite mixture are \(\bar q\) and \(3\sum_jp_j^\infty q_j^2\). A centered Gaussian with variance \(\bar q\) has fourth moment \(3\bar q^2\), and the difference is
\[
 3\sum_jp_j^\infty(q_j-\bar q)^2. \tag{30}
\]
It is strictly positive when two positive limiting weights have different projected variances, so that mixture is not Gaussian.

Finally, stable convergence relative to the terminal label is not implied. For odd \(T\), take \(d=1\), two actions with constant probabilities \((1/2,1/2)\), i.i.d. Rademacher variables \(R_t\), \(Y_t(1)=Y_t(2)=R_t\), and \(g(a,x,y;\theta)=(y-\theta)/2\) on \(\Theta=[-1,1]\). Let the state space be \(\{0\}\), let both regime representatives and every state equal zero, but set \(J=1\) when \(\sum_{t=1}^TR_t>0\) and \(J=2\) otherwise. The score is bounded and linear, \(M_P(\theta)=-\theta\), \(H=-1\), the root is interior and uniformly separated, the constant policy is Lipschitz and satisfies overlap, and both regime covariances equal one. Thus this triangular sequence satisfies every class primitive with \(r_T=\delta_T=0\), both labels have probability \(1/2\), and the exact empirical root is \(T^{-1}\sum_tR_t\).

Let \(h(1)=1\), \(h(2)=-1\), and \(f(x)=\tanh(x)\). The actual joint expectation is
\[
 E\left|\tanh\left(T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^TR_t\right)\right|. \tag{31}
\]
This is bounded away from zero without assuming a limit theorem. Indeed, for \(X_T=T^{-1}(\sum_tR_t)^2\), independence gives \(E[X_T]=1\) and \(E[X_T^2]=3-2/T\le3\). If \(A_T=\{X_T>1/2\}\), then
\[
 1=E[X_T]\le\tfrac12+E[X_T\mathbf 1_{A_T}]
 \le\tfrac12+\sqrt{3P(A_T)},
\]
so \(P(A_T)\ge1/12\), and (31) is at least \(\tanh(1/\sqrt2)/12>0\). Stable convergence to a Gaussian innovation independent of \(J\) would instead force this joint expectation to converge to \(E[h(J)]E[\tanh(Z)]=0\), by symmetry and oddness. This contradiction proves the final negative assertion while leaving the marginal mixture approximation intact.

statements.statement: Using the exact-root linearization on \(E_T\) and carrying its uniformly negligible fallback event \(E_T^c\), uniformly over \(P\in\mathfrak P_T\), \(T^{-1}([S]_T-\langle S\rangle_T)=O_P(T^{-1/2})\), \(\widehat\Omega_T-\Omega_J=O_P(e_T)\), and \(\widehat H_T-H=O_P(e_T)\). Consequently \(\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P(\mathcal E_T^c)\to0\), so the event truncation is asymptotically inactive uniformly, \(\widehat V_T-V_J=O_P(e_T)\), and \(\sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}|P\{T_T^{\mathrm{rqv}}(c)\le z\}-\Phi(z)|\to0\). This is a uniform primitive verification for the present IPW-Z finite-Cesaro-regime class: it derives the self-normalized variance-ratio, invertibility-event, and inverse-QV controls from the common Cesaro attraction and exact-root localization controls. It is not a literal strict tightening of Saco's pointwise AIPW/DML theorem because the estimator and hypothesis classes are different.
statements.justification: The always-defined truncated sandwich tracks the covariance atom selected by the realized Cesaro regime, is asymptotically untruncated uniformly, and removes the Gaussian scale mixture without estimating regime probabilities.
statements.gap: Saco proves a pointwise self-normalized martingale result for a distinct AIPW/DML setup under abstract score-level hypotheses. The present result uniformly verifies the variance-growth, realized-to-predictable-QV, exact-root, feasible-inverse, and truncation controls for the bounded IPW-Z finite-Cesaro-regime class; it does not assert literal inclusion of Saco's published class.
statements.consumer: The result gives a feasible standard-normal Wald procedure for causal excursion contrasts in adaptive mobile-health experiments with path-dependent assignment regimes.
statements.proof_tex:
All stochastic orders below are uniform over \(P\in\mathfrak P_T\) and, when a contrast is present, over \(\|c\|_2=1\). The bounded-score and overlap assumptions give
\[
 \|\xi_t\|_2\le M_\xi:=B/\varepsilon \quad\text{almost surely}. \tag{1}
\]
Define
\[
 D_t=\xi_t\xi_t^\top-E_P[\xi_t\xi_t^\top\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}].
\]
Every entry of \(D_t\) is a martingale difference and
\[
 \|D_t\|_{\mathrm F}\le2M_\xi^2. \tag{2}
\]
Martingale orthogonality, summed over the fixed \(d^2\) entries, yields
\[
 E_P\left\|T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^TD_t\right\|_{\mathrm F}^2
 =T^{-2}\sum_{t=1}^TE_P\|D_t\|_{\mathrm F}^2
 \le \frac{4M_\xi^4}{T}. \tag{3}
\]
Since operator norm is bounded by Frobenius norm, Chebyshev's inequality proves
\[
 T^{-1}([S]_T-\langle S\rangle_T)=O_P(T^{-1/2}). \tag{4}
\]

The exact-root localization and fallback conclusions of \(\mathrm{thm:basin\text{-}stable\text{-}ipwz}\) imply
\[
 \|\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*\|_2=O_P(T^{-1/2}),
 \qquad \partial_\theta G_T(\theta^*)-H=O_P(T^{-1/2}). \tag{5}
\]
For every \(t\), the derivative and overlap bounds give
\[
 \|\widehat\xi_t-\xi_t\|_2
 \le \frac{D_1}{\varepsilon}\|\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*\|_2. \tag{6}
\]
Both scores have norm at most \(M_\xi\), and hence
\[
 \|\widehat\xi_t\widehat\xi_t^\top-\xi_t\xi_t^\top\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \le \frac{2BD_1}{\varepsilon^2}\|\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*\|_2. \tag{7}
\]
Averaging (7), then using (4)--(5) and the predictable-QV expectation bound in \(\mathrm{thm:basin\text{-}stable\text{-}ipwz}\), with Markov's inequality for its last term, gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\widehat\Omega_T-\Omega_J\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 &\le \left\|T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T
 (\widehat\xi_t\widehat\xi_t^\top-\xi_t\xi_t^\top)\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &\quad+\left\|T^{-1}([S]_T-\langle S\rangle_T)\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 +\left\|T^{-1}\langle S\rangle_T-\Omega_J\right\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &=O_P(T^{-1/2}+r_T+\delta_T)=O_P(e_T).
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
On the closed \(\rho\)-ball, the curvature and overlap bounds similarly imply, outside the uniformly negligible fallback event,
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \|\widehat H_T-H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 &\le\|\partial_\theta G_T(\theta^*)-H\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 +\frac{D_2}{\varepsilon}\|\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*\|_2\\
 &=O_P(T^{-1/2})=O_P(e_T).
\end{aligned} \tag{9}
\]
The fallback branch has probability tending uniformly to zero, so (9) holds unconditionally as a uniform-in-probability statement.

For any matrices \(A,B\), the variational definitions of the least singular value and least eigenvalue give \(|\sigma_{\min}(A)-\sigma_{\min}(B)|\le\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) and, for symmetric matrices, \(|\lambda_{\min}(A)-\lambda_{\min}(B)|\le\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\). Thus (8)--(9), \(\sigma_{\min}(H)\ge h_-\), and \(\Omega_J\succeq\omega_-I_d\) imply
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}P(\mathcal E_T^c)\longrightarrow0. \tag{10}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_T\), every inverse is legally evaluated and
\[
 \widehat H_T^{-1}-H^{-1}
 =\widehat H_T^{-1}(H-\widehat H_T)H^{-1},
 \qquad \|\widehat H_T^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le2/h_-. \tag{11}
\]
The first theorem also gives
\[
 \|H^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le h_-^{-1},
 \qquad \|\Omega_J\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le M_\Omega:=KB^2/\varepsilon. \tag{12}
\]
Insert and subtract the three sandwich factors one at a time. Equations (8)--(12) then imply, on \(\mathcal E_T\),
\[
 \widehat H_T^{-1}\widehat\Omega_T\widehat H_T^{-\top}
 -H^{-1}\Omega_JH^{-\top}=O_P(e_T). \tag{13}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_T^c\), \(\widehat V_T=I_d\), while (12) bounds \(V_J\) uniformly. Equation (10) makes this branch uniformly negligible, so (13) and the regime-indexed covariance definition prove
\[
 \widehat V_T-V_J=O_P(e_T). \tag{14}
\]

We now derive the pivotal limit. Fix a unit vector \(c\), and define
\[
 a=H^{-\top}c,\qquad U_t=a^\top\xi_t,\qquad
 A_T^2=\sum_{t=1}^TE_P[U_t^2\mid\mathcal F_{t-1}],\qquad
 Q_T=\sum_{t=1}^TU_t^2. \tag{15}
\]
The upper Jacobian bound from the first theorem and the assumed lower singular-value bound give
\[
 (KD_1)^{-1}\le\|a\|_2\le h_-^{-1},
 \qquad |U_t|\le L:=\frac{B}{\varepsilon h_-}. \tag{16}
\]
The predictable-QV approximation and regime nondegeneracy imply
\[
 \frac{A_T^2}{T}
 =a^\top(T^{-1}\langle S\rangle_T)a
 =a^\top\Omega_Ja+o_P(1),
 \qquad a^\top\Omega_Ja\ge v_0:=\frac{\omega_-}{(KD_1)^2}>0. \tag{17}
\]
Thus \(A_T^2\to\infty\) in probability uniformly. Equation (4) gives
\[
 \frac{Q_T-A_T^2}{T}
 =a^\top T^{-1}([S]_T-\langle S\rangle_T)a
 =O_P(T^{-1/2}), \tag{18}
\]
so (17)--(18) imply \(Q_T/A_T^2\to_P1\) and \(P(Q_T>0)\to1\) uniformly. With \(\delta=2\), (16)--(17) also imply
\[
 A_T^{-4}\sum_{t=1}^TE_P|U_t|^4
 \le A_T^{-4}TL^4\longrightarrow_P0. \tag{19}
\]
Indeed, on the event \(A_T^2/T\ge v_0/2\), the right-hand side is at most \(4L^4/(Tv_0^2)\), and that event has probability tending uniformly to one.

Every triangular array formed by an arbitrary sequence \(P_T\in\mathfrak P_T\) and unit contrasts \(c_T\) therefore satisfies all hypotheses of \(\mathrm{lem:saco\text{-}self\text{-}normalized\text{-}martingale\text{-}clt}\). It follows that
\[
 \frac{a^\top S_T}{\sqrt{a^\top[S]_Ta}}
 =\frac{\sum_{t=1}^TU_t}{\sqrt{Q_T}}\Rightarrow N(0,1). \tag{20}
\]
This convergence is uniform in \(P\) and unit \(c\): otherwise a sequence \((P_T,c_T)\) with Kolmogorov distance bounded away from zero would contradict (20) for that triangular array. Weak convergence to the continuous distribution \(\Phi\) implies Kolmogorov convergence directly: partition the real line at finitely many continuity points so that each intervening \(\Phi\)-increment is arbitrarily small, and use monotonicity of distribution functions between adjacent partition points.

The first theorem gives
\[
 \sqrt T\,c^\top(\widehat\theta_T-\theta^*)
 =-T^{-1/2}a^\top S_T+O_P(e_T). \tag{21}
\]
Furthermore, (4), (8), (14), and \(c^\top V_Jc=a^\top\Omega_Ja\) imply
\[
 c^\top\widehat V_Tc-T^{-1}a^\top[S]_Ta=O_P(e_T). \tag{22}
\]
By (17)--(18), both quantities compared in (22) are at least \(v_0/2\) with probability tending uniformly to one. Division and square roots are therefore legitimate on an event whose probability tends uniformly to one. Since \(e_T\to0\), equations (20)--(22) and
\[
 |\sqrt x-\sqrt y|=\frac{|x-y|}{\sqrt x+\sqrt y}
\]
yield
\[
 T_T^{\mathrm{rqv}}(c)
 =-\frac{a^\top S_T}{\sqrt{a^\top[S]_Ta}}+o_P(1) \tag{23}
\]
uniformly. Applying the same two-sided \(\eta\)-smoothing inclusions used in the first theorem to (20) and (23), together with uniform continuity of \(\Phi\), proves
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}\sup_{z\in\mathbb R}
 \left|P\{T_T^{\mathrm{rqv}}(c)\le z\}-\Phi(z)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{24}
\]

For the causal Wald consequence, define
\[
 I_T(c,\alpha)=\left[\widehat\tau_T-z_{1-\alpha/2}
 \sqrt{\frac{c^\top\widehat V_Tc}{T}},\ 
 \widehat\tau_T+z_{1-\alpha/2}
 \sqrt{\frac{c^\top\widehat V_Tc}{T}}\right].
\]
Because \(\tau=c^\top\theta^*\), the event \(\tau\in I_T(c,\alpha)\) is exactly \(|T_T^{\mathrm{rqv}}(c)|\le z_{1-\alpha/2}\). Hence (24) gives, for every fixed \(\alpha\in(0,1)\),
\[
 \sup_{P\in\mathfrak P_T}\sup_{\|c\|_2=1}
 \left|P\{\tau\in I_T(c,\alpha)\}-(1-\alpha)\right|\longrightarrow0. \tag{25}
\]
No step uses pointwise convergence of \(\eta_t\). The finite label enters only through \(\Omega_J\), and every path approximation is supplied by the uniform Cesaro inequality through the first theorem. Finally, \(\mathrm{lem:saco\text{-}pointwise\text{-}rqv\text{-}pivot}\) concerns a distinct pointwise AIPW/DML setup; accordingly the present derivation verifies the claimed uniform controls but does not assert literal inclusion of that published class.

statements.statement:
Let \(T_\ell\to\infty\) and \(P_\ell\in\mathfrak P_{T_\ell}\) be a sequence or subsequence for which the \(P_\ell\)-specific mixture parameters in Theorem 1 have a fixed support \(\mathcal J_0\), \(p_{P_\ell,j}\to p_j^\infty\), and \(V_{P_\ell,j}\to V_j^\infty\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J_0\). Put \(\mathcal J_\infty=\{j\in\mathcal J_0:p_j^\infty>0\}\). Fix nonzero \(c\) and deterministic positive-definite \(\Sigma\). Then
\[
 \lim_{\ell\to\infty}P_\ell\{\tau\in C_{T_\ell}^{\Sigma}(c,\alpha)\}=1-\alpha
 \quad\text{for every }\alpha\in(0,1)
\]
if and only if \(c^\top V_j^\infty c=c^\top\Sigma c\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J_\infty\). The necessity identifies the law of the limiting finite centered Gaussian scale mixture from coverage at every nominal level; it is not a one-level variance-matching claim.
statements.justification: This theorem exactly characterizes every-level fixed-sandwich validity for one causal contrast along any convergent P-specific mixture subsequence.
statements.gap: Directional-stability work gives sufficient target-specific conditions and Saco highlights random predictable variance; neither gives the finite-mixture every-level converse with vanishing-weight atoms handled explicitly.
statements.consumer: Trial analysts can decide whether a deterministic variance report remains valid for one prespecified HeartSteps excursion-effect contrast even when other directions vary across regimes.
statements.proof_tex:
Set
\[
 q_j=c^\top V_j^\infty c>0,
 \qquad s=c^\top\Sigma c>0. \tag{1}
\]
Positive definiteness and \(c\ne0\) justify all square roots and divisions. By the deterministic interval definition,
\[
 \{\tau\in C_{T_\ell}^{\Sigma}(c,\alpha)\}
 =\left\{\left|\sqrt{T_\ell}\,c^\top(\widehat\theta_{T_\ell}-\theta^*)\right|
 \le z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt s\right\}. \tag{2}
\]
The finite-mixture approximation in \(\mathrm{thm:basin\text{-}stable\text{-}ipwz}\) applies to the triangular sequence \(P_\ell\). The assumed convergence of its weights and covariance matrices, together with continuity of each centered normal distribution function, therefore yields, for \(z=z_{1-\alpha/2}>0\),
\[
 \lim_{\ell\to\infty}P_\ell\{\tau\in C_{T_\ell}^{\Sigma}(c,\alpha)\}
 =\sum_{j\in\mathcal J_\infty}p_j^\infty
 \left\{2\Phi\left(z\sqrt{\frac{s}{q_j}}\right)-1\right\}. \tag{3}
\]
If \(q_j=s\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J_\infty\), the right-hand side is \(2\Phi(z)-1=1-\alpha\), proving sufficiency.

Conversely, suppose the coverage limit equals \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\). As \(\alpha\) ranges over \((0,1)\), \(z_{1-\alpha/2}\) ranges over \((0,\infty)\). Equation (3) then gives
\[
 \sum_{j\in\mathcal J_\infty}p_j^\infty
 \left\{2\Phi\left(z\sqrt{\frac{s}{q_j}}\right)-1\right\}
 =2\Phi(z)-1 \qquad(z>0). \tag{4}
\]
Let \(X\) have law \(\sum_{j\in\mathcal J_\infty}p_j^\infty N(0,q_j)\). Both \(X/\sqrt s\) and a standard Gaussian are symmetric and continuous. Thus equality of their absolute-value distribution functions in (4) for every positive argument implies equality of their full laws. The mixture is finite, so its second and fourth moments exist. Equality of laws gives
\[
 \sum_jp_j^\infty q_j=s,
 \qquad 3\sum_jp_j^\infty q_j^2=3s^2. \tag{5}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \sum_jp_j^\infty(q_j-s)^2
 =\sum_jp_j^\infty q_j^2-2s\sum_jp_j^\infty q_j
 +s^2\sum_jp_j^\infty=0. \tag{6}
\]
Every weight indexed by \(\mathcal J_\infty\) is strictly positive and every summand in (6) is nonnegative, so \(q_j=s\) for every such \(j\). This proves necessity. Requiring every nominal level is essential because it supplies (4) for all \(z>0\); no conclusion here is drawn from one accidental coverage equality.

statements.statement: Along any sequence or subsequence with limiting mixture parameters \((p_j^\infty,V_j^\infty)_{j\in\mathcal J_\infty}\) as in Theorem 3, a single deterministic positive-definite matrix \(\Sigma\) gives asymptotic coverage \(1-\alpha\) for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\) and every nonzero contrast \(c\in\mathbb R^d\) if and only if \(V_j^\infty=\Sigma\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J_\infty\). Equivalently, the limiting selected covariance that equals \(V_j^\infty\) with probability \(p_j^\infty\) is almost surely the deterministic matrix \(\Sigma\). In the fixed-parameter special case this is equivalent to \(V_J=\Sigma\) almost surely. The implication from all projected equalities to matrix equality follows by polarization.
statements.justification: This theorem separates target-specific validity from target-agnostic covariance invariance on the same positive-weight limiting mixture support.
statements.gap: Shen and coauthors distinguish directional from matrix stability on the sufficiency side; the finite-mixture every-level necessity and polarization argument remain unstated.
statements.consumer: Software reporting many adaptive-experiment contrasts can use the theorem to determine whether one fixed covariance matrix is defensible.
statements.proof_tex:
Suppose first that one deterministic positive-definite \(\Sigma\) gives the asserted subsequential coverage for every nonzero \(c\) and every nominal level. By \(\mathrm{thm:contrastwise\text{-}deterministic\text{-}sandwich\text{-}iff}\),
\[
 c^\top(V_j^\infty-\Sigma)c=0
 \qquad\text{for every }c\ne0\text{ and every }j\in\mathcal J_\infty. \tag{1}
\]
Fix \(j\) and let \(A=V_j^\infty-\Sigma\), which is symmetric. Taking \(c=e_r\) in (1) gives \(A_{rr}=0\). For \(r\ne s\), taking \(c=e_r+e_s\) and using the diagonal equalities gives
\[
 0=(e_r+e_s)^\top A(e_r+e_s)=2A_{rs}. \tag{2}
\]
Thus every entry of \(A\) vanishes and \(V_j^\infty=\Sigma\).

Conversely, if \(V_j^\infty=\Sigma\) for every \(j\in\mathcal J_\infty\), then \(c^\top V_j^\infty c=c^\top\Sigma c\) for every nonzero \(c\). The contrastwise theorem gives coverage \(1-\alpha\) for every such \(c\) and every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\).

Let \(V_\infty\) be the random matrix taking value \(V_j^\infty\) with probability \(p_j^\infty\). If all \(V_j^\infty\) equal \(\Sigma\), then \(V_\infty=\Sigma\) almost surely. Conversely, if \(V_\infty=A\) almost surely for a deterministic matrix \(A\), then each event selecting \(j\in\mathcal J_\infty\) has positive probability and forces \(V_j^\infty=A\). In the fixed-parameter case, the identity \(V_J=\sum_j\mathbf 1\{J=j\}V_j\) gives the same equivalence with \(V_\infty\) replaced by \(V_J\). This also supplies the stated polarization implication explicitly through (1)--(2).

statements.statement: For every \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/6)\), the bounded witness \(P^{\dagger}\) belongs at every \(T\ge2\) to a class \(\mathfrak P_T\) with common choices \(B=2\), \(D_1=D_2=1\), \(h_-=1\), \(L_\Pi=1/12\), \(\omega_-=1\), \(\kappa(u)=u\), \(s_\Theta=1\), \(\rho=\varepsilon/8\), \(r_T=1/(2T)\), and \(\delta_T=0\). Specifically, the policy floor is \(1/6\), \(\sup_{a,\theta}\|g(a,X_t,Y_t(a);\theta)\|_2<2\), the derivative and curvature bounds are \(1\) and \(0\), \(M_{P^{\dagger}}(\theta)=-\theta\), every empirical moment admits an exact minimum of zero in \(\Theta\), and \(T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T\|\eta_{t-1}-\bar\eta_J\|_2=1/(2T)\) almost surely. Moreover, \(P^{\dagger}(J=1)=2/5\), \(P^{\dagger}(J=2)=3/5\), so \(\mathcal J=\{1,2\}\); tail selection is exact after the first assignment, \(H=-I_2\), \(\Omega_1=V_1=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\), and \(\Omega_2=V_2=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)\). Hence for \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) and \(c=(1,0)^\top\), \(c^\top V_jc=c^\top\Sigma c=1\) in both positive-mass basins although \(V_1\ne V_2\), so contrastwise deterministic-sandwich validity holds while matrixwise invariance fails.
statements.justification: This elementary bounded construction verifies inside the stated law class that the contrastwise and matrixwise frontiers are logically distinct.
statements.gap: This is a non-novel existence witness, not evidence about the Guo--Xu recursion; its role is to prevent the directional and matrix claims from being conflated by an unattained free-matrix example.
statements.consumer: Applied analysts can retain a valid primary-endpoint interval in a concrete adaptive experiment without claiming that all secondary contrasts share a stable covariance.
statements.proof_tex:
We verify every primitive defining the class. The full-data vectors are i.i.d. because the two Rademacher potential outcomes are independent across occasions and arms and the context is constant. At each occasion the displayed policy is a function of the past-measurable state, and the action is drawn from that logged policy independently of the current potential outcomes, so sequential randomization holds.

At \(\eta=0\) and \(\eta=1\), the arm-probability vectors are
\[
 (2/5,1/4,7/20),\qquad(2/5,1/6,13/30). \tag{1}
\]
Linear interpolation preserves their coordinatewise minima, so every arm probability is at least \(1/6>\varepsilon\). The three coordinate slopes are \(0,-1/12,1/12\), respectively, which proves the policy-Lipschitz condition with \(L_\Pi=1/12\).

For \(\theta\in[-1,1]^2\),
\[
 \sup|Y_t(1)-\theta_1|\le1+\sqrt{2/5}<2,
 \qquad
 \sup|Y_t(2)-\theta_2|\le1+\sqrt{1/2}<2. \tag{2}
\]
Each score has only one possibly nonzero coordinate, so \(B=2\) is valid. The derivative matrices are \(\operatorname{diag}(-1,0)\), \(\operatorname{diag}(0,-1)\), and zero. Their operator norms are at most one and all second derivatives vanish, so \(D_1=D_2=1\) are valid envelopes. Direct expectation gives
\[
 M_{P^\dagger}(\theta)=(-\theta_1,-\theta_2)^\top=-\theta,
 \qquad H=-I_2. \tag{3}
\]
Thus \(\theta^*=0\) is the unique root, \(\|M_{P^\dagger}(\theta)\|_2=\|\theta\|_2\), \(\kappa(u)=u\) is valid, \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial[-1,1]^2)=1\), and \(\sigma_{\min}(H)=1\).

Every realized empirical moment has a zero in \(\Theta\). If arm \(a\in\{1,2\}\) is observed, choose \(\theta_a\) to be the average of its observed outcomes with positive weights \(1/\pi_t(a)\); it belongs to the convex hull of that arm's two possible outcomes and hence to \([-1,1]\). If the arm is never observed, its empirical coordinate moment is identically zero and any coordinate in \([-1,1]\) works. The two coordinates separate, so these choices make \(G_T(\theta)=0\), proving that the empirical moment norm has exact minimum zero.

At the first occasion the state is \(1/2\), and the arm-one probability is \(2/5\). Therefore
\[
 P^\dagger(J=1)=P^\dagger(A_1=1)=2/5,
 \qquad P^\dagger(J=2)=3/5. \tag{4}
\]
For every \(t\ge1\), \(\eta_t=\bar\eta_J\), while \(|\eta_0-\bar\eta_J|=1/2\). Hence
\[
 T^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^T|\eta_{t-1}-\bar\eta_J|=\frac1{2T} \tag{5}
\]
almost surely. The finite regime label is terminally measurable, the Cesaro condition holds with \(r_T=1/(2T)\) and \(\delta_T=0\), and \(e_T=T^{-1/2}+1/(2T)\to0\). Moreover,
\[
 0<\rho=\varepsilon/8<\min\{1,\varepsilon/(4D_2)\}, \tag{6}
\]
so the local radius restriction is satisfied.

At \(\theta^*=0\), only arms one and two contribute to the covariance. Since \(E[Y_t(1)^2]=2/5\) and \(E[Y_t(2)^2]=1/2\),
\[
 \Omega_1=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{2/5}{2/5},\frac{1/2}{1/4}\right)
 =\operatorname{diag}(1,2), \tag{7}
\]
and
\[
 \Omega_2=\operatorname{diag}\left(\frac{2/5}{2/5},\frac{1/2}{1/6}\right)
 =\operatorname{diag}(1,3). \tag{8}
\]
Both dominate \(I_2\), so \(\omega_-=1\) is valid. Since \(H=-I_2\), the sandwich definition gives \(V_j=\Omega_j\). Equations (1)--(8) verify every class condition with constants independent of \(T\).

Finally, for \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(1,2)\) and \(c=(1,0)^\top\),
\[
 c^\top V_1c=c^\top V_2c=c^\top\Sigma c=1,
 \qquad V_1\ne V_2. \tag{9}
\]
The constant sequence has fixed weights \((2/5,3/5)\) and fixed covariance matrices, so it is an instance of the contrastwise and matrixwise theorems. Their conclusions and (9) prove that deterministic-sandwich validity for this contrast coexists with failure of matrix invariance. No assertion about the Guo--Xu recursion is used.

statements.statement:
Consider the bounded-noise Guo--Xu recursion with arbitrary fixed \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2>0\) and deterministic tie arm \(1\). Put \(p=99/100\), \(q=1/100\), and, for \((u,v)\in[q,p]^2\), define
\[
 h(u,v)=\left(\frac{u+16v}{2},\frac{17-u-16v}{2},
                 \frac{u-4v}{4},\frac{-3-u+4v}{24}\right).
\]
For \(t\ge1\), put \(D_{t,a}=\Phi^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,a}\), \(N_{t,a}=b^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,a}\), and \(\Psi_t=(D_{t,1}/t,D_{t,2}/t,N_{t,1}/t,N_{t,2}/t)\). Then \(q^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,a}=O(t^{-1})\) almost surely, \(\Psi_t\) obeys an exact stochastic-approximation recursion with step \(1/(t+1)\), and its affine interpolation is a bounded perturbed solution, hence an asymptotic pseudotrajectory, of the closed convexified inclusion \(\dot\psi\in F(\psi)\) below. Writing \(\Delta(\psi)=n_1/d_1-n_2/d_2\), \(h_+=h(p,q)\), \(h_-=h(q,p)\), \(h_1=h(p,p)\), and \(h_2=h(q,q)\), its graph on \(d_1,d_2>0\) is
\[
 F(\psi)=
 \begin{cases}
  \{h_+-\psi\},&\Delta(\psi)>0,\\
  \{h_--\psi\},&\Delta(\psi)<0,\\
  \operatorname{co}\{h_+,h_-,h_1\}-\psi,&\Delta(\psi)=0,\ d_1<d_2,\\
  \operatorname{co}\{h_+,h_-,h_2\}-\psi,&\Delta(\psi)=0,\ d_1>d_2,\\
  \operatorname{co}\{h_+,h_-,h_1,h_2\}-\psi,&\Delta(\psi)=0,\ d_1=d_2.
 \end{cases}
\]
Every almost-sure normalized-state limit set is internally chain transitive for \(F\) and is contained in the computable parallelogram \(\mathcal C=\{h(u,v):(u,v)\in[q,p]^2\}\); the projected slope limit set is its continuous image under \((d_1,d_2,n_1,n_2)\mapsto(n_1/d_1,n_2/d_2)\).

The smaller inclusion having only \(h_+-\psi\), \(h_--\psi\), and \(\operatorname{co}\{h_+-\psi,h_--\psi\}\) on the switching surface is not a valid unconditional reduction of this recursion. If it were the limiting inclusion, its only internally chain-transitive sets would be the three singletons \(\{h_-\}\), \(\{h(u_0,1-u_0)\}\), and \(\{h_+\}\), where
\[
 u_0=\frac{47+\sqrt{4609}}{150},\qquad
 \frac{N_1}{D_1}=\frac{N_2}{D_2}
 =b_0:=\frac{\sqrt{4609}-91}{1224}
 \quad\text{at }h(u_0,1-u_0).
\]
The correct graph instead has an uncountable family of additional internally chain-transitive singleton equilibria. Explicitly, for
\[
 u\in[u_0,p],\qquad
 v(u)=\frac{3u+18-\sqrt{25u^2-228u+324}}{32},
\]
one has \(h(u,v(u))\in\mathcal C\), equal slope coordinates, first normalized Gram coordinate smaller than the second, and \(0\in F(h(u,v(u)))\). In particular,
\[
 v_*:=v(p)=\frac{2097}{3200}-\frac{3\sqrt{5457}}{640}
\]
gives an equilibrium \(h(p,v_*)\) distinct from \(h_-\), \(h(u_0,1-u_0)\), and \(h_+\). This continuum is an explicit internally-chain-transitive obstruction to a three-candidate conclusion from the standard differential-inclusion route.

For the actual recursion, on \(\mathcal L_+=\{\liminf_t(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1}-\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2})>0\}\) and \(\mathcal L_-=\{\limsup_t(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1}-\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2})<0\}\), respectively,
\[
 (\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1},\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2})^\top
 \longrightarrow
 \left(\frac{19}{46},-\frac{79}{3804}\right)^\top
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \left(-\frac{79}{634},\frac{19}{276}\right)^\top.
\]
Both events have probability bounded away from zero uniformly over \(\eta_0\in\mathsf K_{\mathrm{GX}}\), and the corresponding pathwise Cesaro errors converge to zero. If both slopes have a common-coordinate subsequential limit and \((u,v)\) is a simultaneous subsequential limit of the empirical conditional arm-\(1\) rates, then necessarily
\[
 u^2+12uv-21u-64v^2+72v=0.
\]
The relation \(v=1-u\), and hence the candidate \((u_0,b_0)\), is justified only if same-arm switching-layer occupation is separately excluded; the exact recursion does not provide that exclusion. Consequently, this argument proves neither finite almost-sure tail selection nor zero probability of switching-surface convergence. It also proves no compact-initial-set uniform attraction moduli \(r_T(K_0),\delta_T(K_0)\). These are dynamics-only conclusions: they assert neither membership in \(\mathfrak P_T\) nor applicability of any inference theorem.
statements.justification: The normalized sufficient-statistic recursion gives the strongest rigorous dynamics certificate currently available: it proves the two separated limits and exposes an uncountable switching-equilibrium obstruction in the correct limiting differential inclusion.
statements.gap: The differential-inclusion limit set need not be one of three candidates because the vanishing UCB bonus produces same-arm modes inside the shrinking switching layer. Actual selection within that layer, zero probability of switching convergence, and compact-initial-set uniform attraction still require quantitative escape and equicontinuity estimates not supplied here.
statements.consumer: The result prevents the bounded Guo--Xu analogue from being used as a certified two-basin inference witness while identifying the exact normalized-state graph and the additional dynamics that a future separatrix analysis must control.
statements.proof_tex:
Write \(\mu _1=1/2\), \(\mu _2=1/12\), \(p=99/100\), \(q=1/100\), and \(C_{t,a}=\mathbf 1\{A_t=a\}\).  The recursion in \(\textnormal{def:guoxu-recursion}\) gives, for every \(t\geq 1\),
\[
 D_{t,a}=1+\sum_{s=1}^t C_{s,a}X_s^2,\qquad
 N_{t,a}=\eta_{0,a}+\sum_{s=1}^t C_{s,a}X_s(\mu_a+\sigma_aR_{s,a}),\qquad
 \widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,a}=\frac{N_{t,a}}{D_{t,a}}. \tag{1}
\]
The clipped randomization assigns either arm with conditional probability at least \(q\).  Because \(X_s\) is independent of \(\mathcal F_{s-1}\) and uniform on \(\{-4,1\}\),
\[
 E[C_{s,a}X_s^2\mid\mathcal F_{s-1}]
 \geq qE[X_s^2]=\frac{17}{200}. \tag{2}
\]
We first record the elementary bounded-martingale argument used repeatedly below.  If \((U_s)\) is a scalar martingale-difference sequence with \(|U_s|\leq L\), expansion of the square and iterated conditional expectation make the cross terms zero, so \(E(\sum_{s\leq n}U_s)^2\leq L^2n\).  At \(n=k^2\), the pointwise inequality \(\mathbf 1\{|x|>a\}\leq x^2/a^2\) gives
\[
 P\left(\left|\sum_{s\leq k^2}U_s\right|>\epsilon k^2\right)
 \leq \frac{L^2}{\epsilon^2k^2}.
\]
For every \(K\), the probability that one of these events occurs for some \(k\geq K\) is at most \(L^2\epsilon^{-2}\sum_{k\geq K}k^{-2}\), which tends to zero as \(K\to\infty\).  Thus only finitely many occur almost surely and \(k^{-2}\sum_{s\leq k^2}U_s\to0\).  The at most \(2k+1\) bounded increments between \(k^2\) and \((k+1)^2\) fill the gaps, proving \(n^{-1}\sum_{s\leq n}U_s\to0\) almost surely.

Apply this result to \(C_{s,a}X_s^2-E[C_{s,a}X_s^2\mid\mathcal F_{s-1}]\).  Equations (1)--(2) yield
\[
 \liminf_{t\to\infty}\frac{D_{t,a}}t\geq\frac{17}{200},
 \qquad q^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,a}=D_{t,a}^{-1}=O(t^{-1})
 \quad\text{almost surely}. \tag{3}
\]
The same argument applies to \(C_{s,a}X_sR_{s,a}\): by the ordering in \(\textnormal{def:guoxu-recursion}\), the action is randomized before the reward innovation is observed, and that innovation is conditionally centered.  Hence
\[
 t^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^tC_{s,a}X_sR_{s,a}\longrightarrow0
 \quad\text{almost surely}. \tag{4}
\]
Moreover, (1) expresses each slope as a convex combination of its initial value \(\eta_{0,a}\) and the observed ratios \(Y_s(a)/X_s\), with weights \(1\) and \(C_{s,a}X_s^2\).  The envelope \(M_{\mathrm{GX}}\) therefore bounds both slopes.  Together with bounded \(X_s\) and bounded Rademacher rewards, this bounds every coordinate of \(\Psi_t\); by (3), both normalized Gram coordinates are eventually bounded away from zero.

Define
\[
 U_{t+1}=\bigl(C_{t+1,1}X_{t+1}^2,C_{t+1,2}X_{t+1}^2,
 C_{t+1,1}X_{t+1}Y_{t+1}(1),C_{t+1,2}X_{t+1}Y_{t+1}(2)\bigr).
\]
Dividing the four sufficient-statistic updates by \(t+1\) gives the exact stochastic-approximation recursion
\[
 \Psi_{t+1}-\Psi_t=\frac1{t+1}(U_{t+1}-\Psi_t). \tag{5}
\]
Conditional on \(\mathcal F_t\), let \(u_t\) and \(v_t\) be the arm-one assignment probabilities at contexts \(1\) and \(-4\), respectively.  Conditional centering of the rewards and direct averaging over the two equally likely contexts give
\[
 E[U_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]=h(u_t,v_t), \tag{6}
\]
because the four coordinates on the right are
\[
 \frac{u_t+16v_t}{2},\qquad \frac{17-u_t-16v_t}{2},\qquad
 \mu_1\frac{u_t-4v_t}{2},\qquad
 \mu_2\frac{-3-u_t+4v_t}{2}.
\]
This is precisely the displayed formula for \(h\).

For \(\psi=(d_1,d_2,n_1,n_2)\), put \(\Delta(\psi)=n_1/d_1-n_2/d_2\).  At the current normalized state,
\[
 b_t:=\sqrt{q^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1}}-\sqrt{q^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2}}
 =t^{-1/2}\bigl(d_{t,1}^{-1/2}-d_{t,2}^{-1/2}\bigr). \tag{7}
\]
The arm-one minus arm-two UCB index has the sign of \(\Delta(\Psi_t)+b_t\) at context \(1\), and the sign of \(b_t-\Delta(\Psi_t)\) at context \(-4\).  Equation (3) gives \(|b_t|=O(t^{-1/2})\).  Consequently, away from \(\Delta=0\), the two greedy choices are eventually opposite: \((u_t,v_t)=(p,q)\) for \(\Delta>0\), and \((u_t,v_t)=(q,p)\) for \(\Delta<0\).  On \(\Delta=0\), equation (7) has the sign of \(d_2-d_1\).  Thus both contexts make arm one greedy when \(d_1<d_2\), both make arm two greedy when \(d_1>d_2\), and the specified deterministic tie rule makes arm one greedy when \(d_1=d_2\).  The corresponding conditional means are \(h_1,h_2,h_1\), respectively.

This calculation gives the asserted closed convexified graph.  To verify the perturbation condition explicitly, observe that a same-arm mode can occur off the switching surface only if \(|\Delta(\Psi_t)|\leq |b_t|\).  On the eventual compact region already obtained, replace \(n_1\) by \(n_1-d_1\Delta(\Psi_t)\), leaving the other coordinates fixed.  The resulting point lies on \(\Delta=0\) and is within a fixed multiple of \(|\Delta(\Psi_t)|\) of \(\Psi_t\).  Therefore, for a deterministic \(c_0<\infty\),
\[
 E[U_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]-\Psi_t\in F^{\delta_t}(\Psi_t),
 \qquad \delta_t=c_0t^{-1/2}\longrightarrow0, \tag{8}
\]
where \(F^\delta\) denotes the graph enlargement.  The atoms \(h_+\) and \(h_-\) at every switching point make the graph closed under approach from the two open half-spaces; the atom \(h_1\), respectively \(h_2\), records approach within the switching layer when \(d_1<d_2\), respectively \(d_1>d_2\); and all four atoms at \(d_1=d_2\) close the remaining approaches.  Hence the displayed graph has nonempty compact convex values and is closed.  Its velocities have linear growth because its four atoms are fixed.  Outside a compact convex region containing the eventual trajectory, compose the atom correspondence with metric projection and retain the term \(-\psi\); this supplies a global extension with the same properties without changing the eventual dynamics.

Let \(M_{t+1}=U_{t+1}-E[U_{t+1}\mid\mathcal F_t]\) and \(\gamma_t=1/t\).  Each coordinate is a bounded martingale difference.  Stopping its weighted partial sum at the first crossing of \(\epsilon\) and using orthogonality of the stopped increments gives, for every coordinate and every \(j\),
\[
 P\left\{\sup_{k\geq2^j}\left|\sum_{s=2^j}^k\gamma_{s+1}M_{s+1}\right|>\epsilon\right\}
 \leq \frac{C}{\epsilon^2}\sum_{s=2^j}^{\infty}\gamma_{s+1}^2
 \leq\frac{C'}{\epsilon^22^j}. \tag{9}
\]
The probability that one of the events in (9) occurs for some \(j\geq J\) is at most \(C'\epsilon^{-2}\sum_{j\geq J}2^{-j}\), which tends to zero.  Thus the weighted martingale tails vanish almost surely, uniformly over every bounded interval of stochastic-approximation time.  Equations (5), (8), and (9), together with boundedness of \(\Psi_t\), verify the bounded-perturbed-solution hypotheses of \(\textnormal{lem:bhs-perturbed-limit-set}\).  That lemma makes the affine interpolation an asymptotic pseudotrajectory and makes its limit set internally chain transitive.

Let
\[
 \mathcal C=h([q,p]^2)=\operatorname{co}\{h_+,h_-,h_1,h_2\}.
\]
Every velocity in \(F(\psi)\) is \(z-\psi\) for some \(z\in\mathcal C\).  If \(P_{\mathcal C}\psi\) is the Euclidean projection and \(V(\psi)=\operatorname{dist}(\psi,\mathcal C)^2\), the projection inequality gives, along every solution and for almost every time outside \(\mathcal C\),
\[
 \frac{d}{ds}V(\psi(s))
 =2(\psi-P_{\mathcal C}\psi)^\top(z-\psi)
 \leq-2\|\psi-P_{\mathcal C}\psi\|_2^2=-2V(\psi). \tag{10}
\]
If a solution starts in \(\mathcal C\), variation of constants writes it as a convex combination of its initial point and a weighted average of points \(z(s)\in\mathcal C\); hence \(\mathcal C\) is positively invariant.  Thus \(V\) is a continuous Lyapunov function for \(\mathcal C\), and \(V(\mathcal C)=\{0\}\) has empty interior.  By \(\textnormal{lem:bhs-lyapunov-ict}\), every internally chain-transitive normalized-state limit set lies in \(\mathcal C\).  Equation (3) keeps \(d_1,d_2\) positive on that limit set, so the slope projection \((d_1,d_2,n_1,n_2)\mapsto(n_1/d_1,n_2/d_2)\) is continuous there.  This proves the first paragraph of the claim.

We next identify exactly what the tempting two-mode inclusion would imply.  Let \(\mathcal C_0=\operatorname{co}\{h_-,h_+\}\) and write its points uniquely as \(h_-+\lambda(h_+-h_-)\), \(0\leq\lambda\leq1\).  Equivalently,
\[
 u=q+(p-q)\lambda,\qquad v=p-(p-q)\lambda=1-u. \tag{11}
\]
Cross-multiplication is legitimate because both Gram coordinates are positive, and direct expansion gives
\[
 \Delta(h(u,v))=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 f(u,v):=u^2+12uv-21u-64v^2+72v=0; \tag{12}
\]
indeed, after multiplication by the positive common denominator, the numerator of the slope difference is \(-5f(u,v)\).  Substitution of \(v=1-u\) yields \(f(u,1-u)=-75u^2+47u+8\).  Its unique root in \([q,p]\) is
\[
 u_0=\frac{47+\sqrt{4609}}{150},
\]
and substitution into either slope ratio gives \(b_0=(\sqrt{4609}-91)/1224\).

On \(\mathcal C_0\), the two-mode inclusion reduces to
\[
 \dot\lambda=-\lambda\quad(\lambda<\lambda_0),\qquad
 \dot\lambda=1-\lambda\quad(\lambda>\lambda_0),\qquad
 \dot\lambda\in[-\lambda_0,1-\lambda_0]\quad(\lambda=\lambda_0), \tag{13}
\]
where \(u_0=q+(p-q)\lambda_0\).  Distance squared to \(\mathcal C_0\) first confines every internally chain-transitive set to the segment by the argument of (10).  On the segment, the continuous function
\[
 W(\lambda)=
 \begin{cases}
 \lambda/\lambda_0,&0\leq\lambda\leq\lambda_0,\\
 (1-\lambda)/(1-\lambda_0),&\lambda_0\leq\lambda\leq1
 \end{cases}
\]
strictly decreases along every nonconstant solution outside \(\{0,\lambda_0,1\}\) and never increases from those three points.  Since \(W(\{0,\lambda_0,1\})=\{0,1\}\) has empty interior, \(\textnormal{lem:bhs-lyapunov-ict}\) puts every internally chain-transitive set inside \(\{0,\lambda_0,1\}\) with \(W\) constant.  The set \(\{0,1\}\) is not internally chain transitive: for \(\epsilon<1/3\), the solutions from its endpoints are constant, so no \((\epsilon,S)\)-chain contained in that two-point set can travel from one endpoint to the other.  Thus only the three asserted singletons are internally chain transitive for the smaller inclusion.

That smaller graph cannot approximate the recursion uniformly near the switching surface.  If \(\Delta=0\) and \(d_1<d_2\), equation (7) makes arm one greedy at both contexts and the conditional mean is \(h_1\).  But \(h_1\notin\mathcal C_0\): the affine map \((u,v)\mapsto h(u,v)\) is injective, every parameter pair on \(\mathcal C_0\) satisfies \(u+v=1\), and \(h_1\) corresponds to \((p,p)\), whose sum is \(2p\neq1\).  Compactness therefore gives \(\operatorname{dist}(h_1,\mathcal C_0)>0\).  The \(O(t^{-1/2})\) bonus cannot be discarded uniformly in the \(O(t^{-1/2})\) switching layer.

The extra internally chain-transitive sets of the correct graph are computable.  Solving (12) for its smaller \(v\)-root gives
\[
 v(u)=\frac{3u+18-\sqrt{25u^2-228u+324}}{32}. \tag{14}
\]
For \(u\in[u_0,p]\), substitution verifies \(f(u,v(u))=0\) and \(v(u_0)=1-u_0\).  Direct differentiation gives
\[
 v'(u)=\frac1{32}\left(3+\frac{228-50u}{2\sqrt{25u^2-228u+324}}\right)>0, \tag{15}
\]
because \(u\leq p<1\).  The elementary bounds \(67<\sqrt{4609}<68\) and \(73<\sqrt{5457}<74\) imply
\[
 0.23<v(u_0)<0.24,\qquad 0.308<v(p)<0.314.
\]
Consequently \(q<u,v(u)<p\), \(u+v(u)\geq1\), and
\[
 u+16v(u)\leq p+16v(p)<p+16(0.314)<6.014<\frac{17}{2}. \tag{16}
\]
The first two inequalities put \((u,v(u))\) in the triangle with vertices \((p,q),(q,p),(p,p)\), while (16) says that the first Gram coordinate of \(h(u,v(u))\) is smaller than the second.  Therefore
\[
 h(u,v(u))\in\operatorname{co}\{h_+,h_-,h_1\},\qquad
 \Delta(h(u,v(u)))=0,\qquad 0\in F(h(u,v(u))). \tag{17}
\]
Each singleton in (17) is an equilibrium and hence internally chain transitive.  The map \(h\) is injective because the two linear forms \(u+16v\) and \(u-4v\) have nonzero determinant; the family is therefore uncountable.  At \(u=p\), equation (14) simplifies to
\[
 v(p)=\frac{2097}{3200}-\frac{3\sqrt{5457}}{640}=v_*,
\]
and the bounds above show that this equilibrium differs from the three two-mode candidates.  This proves the stated obstruction.

It remains to separate what the exact recursion itself establishes from what the enlarged inclusion merely permits.  Put \(\Delta_t=\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1}-\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2}\).  On \(\mathcal L_+\), equation (3) makes the bonus vanish while \(\Delta_t\) is eventually bounded below by a positive constant.  Hence eventually arm one is greedy at context \(1\) and arm two at context \(-4\).  Applying the bounded martingale law proved above to the four context--action counts, and using (4) for the reward noise, gives
\[
 \frac1t(D_{t,1},D_{t,2},N_{t,1},N_{t,2})
 \longrightarrow h_+=\left(\frac{23}{40},\frac{317}{40},\frac{19}{80},-\frac{79}{480}\right). \tag{18}
\]
Equations (1) and (18) yield the first displayed slope limit.  The identical argument on \(\mathcal L_-\) gives
\[
 \frac1t(D_{t,1},D_{t,2},N_{t,1},N_{t,2})
 \longrightarrow h_-=\left(\frac{317}{40},\frac{23}{40},-\frac{79}{80},\frac{19}{480}\right), \tag{19}
\]
and hence the second displayed slope limit.  The limiting slope gaps are, respectively,
\[
 \frac{19}{46}+\frac{79}{3804}=
 \frac{37955}{87492}>0,
 \qquad
 -\frac{79}{634}-\frac{19}{276}=-\frac{16925}{87492}<0. \tag{20}
\]

We now prove the uniform positive-probability assertion rather than infer it from the differential inclusion.  Fix a sufficiently large even \(n\).  For the positive regime, prescribe a length-\(2n\) history consisting first of \(n\) observations with \(X=1,A=1\), then \(n\) observations with \(X=-4,A=2\), and prescribe equally many positive and negative Rademacher signs for each selected arm.  Each prescribed context has probability \(1/2\), each prescribed action has conditional probability at least \(q\), and each prescribed relevant sign has probability \(1/2\).  Thus this history has probability at least \((q/4)^{2n}\), uniformly over \(\eta_0\in[-1,1]^2\).  At its end the slopes are exactly
\[
 \frac{\eta_{0,1}+n/2}{1+n},\qquad
 \frac{\eta_{0,2}-n/3}{1+16n}, \tag{21}
\]
which converge uniformly in \(\eta_0\) to \(1/2\) and \(-1/48\), and both inverse Gram coordinates are \(O(n^{-1})\).

Consider after this prefix the reference policy that makes arm one greedy at context \(1\) and arm two greedy at context \(-4\).  After \(k\) further steps, its conditional-mean sufficient statistics are obtained by adding \(kh_+\) to the four terminal statistics in (21).  Each resulting armwise slope is a denominator-weighted average of its terminal slope and the corresponding ratio in \(h_+\).  By (20)--(21), there are constants \(\gamma_0>0\) and \(n_0<\infty\), independent of \(\eta_0\), such that for \(n\geq n_0\) these two reference slopes differ by at least \(3\gamma_0\) for every \(k\geq0\).  Their Gram coordinates are at least a fixed positive multiple of \(n+k\), so the absolute difference of their UCB bonuses is at most \(C(n+k)^{-1/2}\).  Increasing \(n_0\) makes this bound at most \(\gamma_0\).

Couple the actual rule and this reference rule with the same contexts, rewards, and randomization uniforms, and let \(\zeta\) be the first future occasion at which their greedy arms differ.  Up to the state immediately before \(\zeta\), subtracting the conditional mean \(h_+\) from each sufficient-statistic increment gives four stopped martingales with a common bounded-increment constant depending only on the fixed \(\sigma_1,\sigma_2\).  The stopped-process maximal inequality and a union bound over the dyadic blocks \(2^jn\leq n+k<2^{j+1}n\) yield, for every fixed \(\gamma>0\),
\[
 P\left(\sup_{k\geq0}\frac{\|M_{k\wedge(\zeta-1)}\|_\infty}{n+k}>\gamma
 \mathrel{\Big|}\text{the prescribed prefix}\right)
 \leq \sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{C}{\gamma^22^jn}
 =\frac{C_\gamma}{n}. \tag{22}
\]
Indeed, a crossing on the \(j\)-th block requires a stopped partial sum of size at least \(\gamma2^jn\), whereas orthogonality bounds its second moment by a constant times \(2^{j+1}n\), which gives the displayed summand.

Because all reference denominators are bounded below by a constant times \(n+k\), the ratio map is uniformly Lipschitz under the relative perturbation in (22).  Choose \(\gamma\) small enough both to preserve a positive constant lower bound for the perturbed denominators and to change the slope gap by at most \(\gamma_0\).  The same denominator bound makes the actual bonus difference \(O((n+k)^{-1/2})\); enlarge \(n_0\) once more so that it is at most \(\gamma_0\).  On the complementary event in (22), the actual slope gap is therefore at least \(2\gamma_0\), while its bonus difference is at most \(\gamma_0\).  At a putative first exit, the UCB index difference is consequently positive at context \(1\) and negative at context \(-4\), so the actual greedy arms still equal the reference greedy arms, a contradiction.  Thus \(\zeta=\infty\) on that event.  Equation (18), now applied under the reference policy, implies \(\mathcal L_+\).  Taking \(n\) still larger so that \(C_\gamma/n\leq1/2\) proves
\[
 \inf_{\eta_0\in\mathsf K_{\mathrm{GX}}}P_{\eta_0}(\mathcal L_+)
 \geq \frac12(q/4)^{2n}>0. \tag{23}
\]
For the negative regime, prescribe first \(n\) observations with \(X=-4,A=1\), then \(n\) with \(X=1,A=2\), again balancing the selected Rademacher signs.  The terminal slopes converge uniformly to \(-1/8\) and \(1/12\); the conditional-mean continuation adds \(kh_-\), and the second strict gap in (20) supplies the same stopped-martingale bootstrap.  Consequently
\[
 \inf_{\eta_0\in\mathsf K_{\mathrm{GX}}}P_{\eta_0}(\mathcal L_-)>0. \tag{24}
\]
On either event the corresponding slope sequence converges.  If \(\beta^+\) and \(\beta^-\) denote the two displayed deterministic limits, split each average at a fixed index after which every summand is at most an arbitrary \(\epsilon>0\); the fixed prefix divided by \(T\) vanishes.  Therefore, respectively,
\[
 \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\left\|\bigl(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1},\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2}\bigr)^\top-\beta^+\right\|_2\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad
 \frac1T\sum_{t=1}^T\left\|\bigl(\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,1},\widehat\beta^{\mathrm{GX}}_{t,2}\bigr)^\top-\beta^-\right\|_2\longrightarrow0.
\]
This is the asserted pathwise Cesaro-error conclusion.

Finally, define the empirical context-specific arm-one rates
\[
 u_T=\frac2T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{X_t=1,A_t=1\},\qquad
 v_T=\frac2T\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbf1\{X_t=-4,A_t=1\}.
\]
The conditional arm-one probability at either context is always in \([q,p]\).  Applying the bounded martingale law to each centered context--action indicator, and to each centered context indicator, shows that every subsequential limit of \((u_T,v_T)\) lies in \([q,p]^2\).  If along a common subsequence both slopes tend to a common coordinate and \((u_T,v_T)\to(u,v)\), then (1), (4), and the context-count law give
\[
 \frac1T(D_{T,1},D_{T,2},N_{T,1},N_{T,2})\longrightarrow h(u,v).
\]
The denominators in this limit are positive because \((u,v)\in[q,p]^2\).  Equality of the two limiting slope ratios is therefore equivalent, by (12), to
\[
 u^2+12uv-21u-64v^2+72v=0.
\]
If same-arm switching-layer occupation is excluded, only the two opposite-context modes remain and (11) forces \(v=1-u\), producing \((u_0,b_0)\).  But (7) and the continuum in (14)--(17) show that this exclusion is not a consequence of the exact recursion or of the differential-inclusion theorem: same-arm modes survive throughout the shrinking switching layer.  The graph is discontinuous there, and the preceding argument supplies neither an avoidance estimate for switching-surface convergence nor a quantitative hitting, escape, or equicontinuity estimate uniform over compact initial sets.  It therefore establishes neither finite almost-sure tail selection nor zero switching-surface probability, and it does not establish compact-uniform moduli \(r_T(K_0),\delta_T(K_0)\).  Since membership in \(\mathfrak P_T\) requires precisely such tail-selection and uniform-attraction properties, no membership or inference conclusion is asserted.  This proves all parts of the theorem.

Let \(p\in[1,\infty)\), \(\gamma>0\), and let \((X_i,\mathcal G_i)_{i=1}^n\) be a scalar martingale-difference sequence with \(n\ge2\) and \(\max_i\|X_i\|_\infty\le\gamma\). Put \(s^2=\sum_{i=1}^nE[X_i^2]\), \(V^2=s^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^nE[X_i^2\mid\mathcal G_{i-1}]\), and \(D=\sup_x|P\{s^{-1}\sum_iX_i\le x\}-\Phi(x)|\). There is a constant \(C_{p,\gamma}\) such that
\[
D\le C_{p,\gamma}\left\{\frac{n\log n}{s^3}+\left(\|V^2-1\|_p^p+s^{-2p}\right)^{1/(2p+1)}\right\}.
\]

Let \((X_{n,t},\mathcal G_{n,t})_{t=1}^{k_n}\) be a scalar martingale-difference array, \(S_n=\sum_tX_{n,t}\), \(Q_n=\sum_tX_{n,t}^2\), and \(A_n^2=\sum_tE[X_{n,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{n,t-1}]\). If \(A_n^2\to\infty\) in probability, \(P(Q_n>0)\to1\), \(Q_n/A_n^2\to1\) in probability, and for some \(\delta>0\),
\[
 A_n^{-(2+\delta)}\sum_tE[|X_{n,t}|^{2+\delta}]\to0,
\]
then \(S_n/\sqrt{Q_n}\Rightarrow N(0,1)\).

Let \((X_{T,t},\mathcal G_{T,t})_{t=1}^T\) be a scalar martingale-difference triangular array under \(P\), let \(0\le k_T<T\), and suppose \(|X_{T,t}|\le L<\infty\) almost surely. Let \(\lambda_T\) be \(\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\)-measurable and satisfy \(0<v_-\le\lambda_T\le v_+<\infty\) almost surely. If
\[
 \Delta_T:=E_P\left|T^{-1}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T
 E_P[X_{T,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}]-\lambda_T\right|\longrightarrow0,
\]
then
\[
 \sup_{z\in\mathbb R}\left|P\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -E_P\Phi\left(\frac{z}{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|\longrightarrow0.
\]
The conclusion is uniform over any collection of arrays having common \(L,v_-,v_+\) and a common upper bound on \(\Delta_T\) that tends to zero.
statements.proof_tex:
Put
\[
 Q_T=T^{-1}\sum_{t=k_T+1}^T E_P[X_{T,t}^2\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}].
\]
Fix \(\eta>0\) and partition \([v_-,v_+]\) into finitely many Borel intervals \(I_r\) of diameter at most \(\eta\). The events \(B_r=\{\lambda_T\in I_r\}\) belong to \(\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\). Choose \(\lambda_r\in I_r\). For every cell of positive probability, let \(P_r=P(\,\cdot\mid B_r)\). Because \(B_r\in\mathcal G_{T,k_T}\subseteq\mathcal G_{T,t-1}\) for \(t>k_T\), the defining martingale-difference equality remains valid under \(P_r\):
\[
 E_{P_r}[X_{T,t}\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}]
 =\frac{E_P[\mathbf 1_{B_r}X_{T,t}\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1}]}{P(B_r\mid\mathcal G_{T,t-1})}=0.
\]
Here the displayed ratio is read only on \(B_r\), where its denominator is one; equivalently, the equality follows directly by testing against bounded \(\mathcal G_{T,t-1}\)-measurable functions under the conditional law.

Define
\[
 d_r=E_{P_r}|Q_T-\lambda_T|+\eta,
 \qquad q_r=E_{P_r}Q_T,
 \qquad s_r^2=Tq_r.
\]
Since \(|\lambda_T-\lambda_r|\le\eta\) on \(B_r\),
\[
 |q_r-\lambda_r|\le d_r,
 \qquad
 \sum_rP(B_r)d_r\le\Delta_T+\eta.
\]
Call a cell good when \(d_r\le v_-/2\). The total probability of the bad cells is at most \(2(\Delta_T+\eta)/v_-\). On a good cell, \(q_r\ge v_-/2\), and the normalized predictable quadratic variation in the cited Mourrat bound is \(V_r^2=Q_T/q_r\). Therefore
\[
 E_{P_r}|V_r^2-1|
 \le q_r^{-1}E_{P_r}|Q_T-q_r|
 \le \frac{4d_r}{v_-}.
\]
The increments are bounded by \(L\), the number of tail increments is at most \(T\), and \(s_r^2\ge Tv_-/2\). Apply the cited quantitative bound \(\mathrm{lem:mourrat\text{-}bounded\text{-}martingale\text{-}clt}\) with \(p=1\) under \(P_r\). It gives a common constant \(C\) such that
\[
 \sup_z\left|P_r\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t>k_T}X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{q_r}}\right)\right|
 \le C\left\{\frac{\log T}{\sqrt T}+\left(d_r+T^{-1}\right)^{1/3}\right\}
\]
on every good cell. The normal scale family is uniformly Lipschitz in its variance on \([v_-/2,2v_+]\): indeed, with \(\phi\) the standard normal density,
\[
 \sup_z\left|\frac{\partial}{\partial q}\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt q}\right)\right|
 =\sup_u\frac{|u|\phi(u)}{2q}\le C_{v_-}.
\]
Consequently, on a good cell,
\[
 \sup_z\left|\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{q_r}}\right)
 -E_{P_r}\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|
 \le C_{v_-}d_r.
\]
After multiplying by \(P(B_r)\), summing, bounding each bad-cell discrepancy by one, and using concavity of \(x^{1/3}\), we obtain
\[
 \sup_z\left|P\left\{T^{-1/2}\sum_{t>k_T}X_{T,t}\le z\right\}
 -E_P\Phi\left(\frac z{\sqrt{\lambda_T}}\right)\right|
 \le C\left\{\frac{\log T}{\sqrt T}+\left(\Delta_T+\eta+T^{-1}\right)^{1/3}
 +\Delta_T+\eta\right\}.
\]
Taking, for example, \(\eta=T^{-1}\) proves the assertion. Every constant in the display depends only on \(L,v_-,v_+\), which also proves the stated uniformity.
statements.justification: This conditioning-free finite-partition lemma is the glue that turns an early-measurable variance proxy into a marginal Gaussian-mixture approximation.
statements.gap: Mourrat supplies the quantitative deterministic-variance martingale bound; the finite-partition adaptation to a random early-measurable variance is derived here.
statements.consumer: Theorem 1 uses the lemma to obtain the strongest label-free law allowed by the attraction primitives.

sampling_model.design: Known, logged, context-dependent randomization \(\pi_t(a\mid X_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})=\Pi(a\mid X_t,\eta_{t-1})\) updated by a history-measurable recursion.
sampling_model.units: A growing sequence of independent full-data decision occasions \(W_t\); the inferential dependence is induced by the common adaptive policy state.
sampling_model.treatment: A finite action set with sequential randomization and consistency \(Y_t=Y_t(A_t)\).
sampling_model.overlap: Known clipping floor \(\pi_t(a\mid X_t,\mathcal F_{t-1})\ge\varepsilon\), common over the triangular-array law class.
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: No outcome-model nuisance is required for identification; a preliminary moment-norm minimizer localizes a total measurable exact-root selector, the Z-Jacobian and realized score quadratic variation are estimated on the observed adaptive path, and the sandwich is set to \(I_d\) off the common invertibility event.

tldr: The field-tier contribution is a conditional finite-attractor theorem bundle for adaptive causal IPW-Z inference. Under common score, derivative, Jacobian-lower-bound, policy, covariance-lower-bound, root-separation, attraction, and local root-search envelopes, with attainable basins defined as the positive-mass support of the tail selector, the bundle derives a basin-stable finite Gaussian mixture with predictable-QV error controlled by \(r_T+\delta_T\), proves that an always-defined same-path realized-QV sandwich is uniformly pivotal and asymptotically untruncated, and gives exact deterministic-sandwich boundaries: every-level validity for one contrast holds if and only if that contrast's variance is basin-invariant, while validity for all contrasts holds if and only if the full covariance is deterministic. Theorem 2 has one direct strict-tightening comparator, Saco's pointwise realized-QV result; the remaining named papers provide motivation, ingredients, or orthogonal regimes rather than a second strict frontier. An elementary bounded two-basin law verifies that contrastwise invariance need not imply matrix invariance. The slope-projected limit set of the augmented bounded Guo--Xu Markov chain remains an open dynamics question with no class-membership or inference claim.

project_justification.gap: Saco supplies the one direct pointwise realized-QV comparator, but not uniform verification over an endogenous finite-attractor class. Guo--Xu and Shen and coauthors supply adjacent stable-policy and directional-stability results, Han studies continuous SDE-invariant Thompson-sampling pull proportions and raw-arm-mean inference, and Leiner, Dunn, and Ramdas study stationary-evaluation-policy off-policy M-estimation with flexible variance stabilization under unstable logging. Zhang, Janson, and Murphy instead study pooled longitudinal adaptive sampling with Z-estimation and an adaptive sandwich estimator in a fixed-within-user, growing-participant regime. Existing stochastic-approximation results control lock-in only after entry into an attraction domain, and the Guo--Xu two-mode example remains numerical.
project_justification.niche: The unoccupied field-tier object is a conditional recursion-level uniform limit theory that preserves the random basin, validates a finite-sample-defined same-path studentizer, and states exact contrastwise and matrixwise boundaries for deterministic-sandwich inference. The absence of a second direct strict-tightening comparator caps the positioning at field tier, which is the requested floor and achieved target.
project_justification.fill: The publishable contribution is the conditional finite-attractor theorem bundle: a basin-stable causal IPW-Z finite Gaussian mixture, a uniformly feasible same-path realized-QV pivot, and exact contrastwise and matrixwise deterministic-sandwich boundaries. A finite-attractor class indexed by common score, derivative, Jacobian lower, policy, covariance lower, root-separation, attraction, and local root-search envelopes converts policy dynamics into predictable-QV control with error \(r_T+\delta_T\); its attainable-basin index set is the positive-mass support of the tail selector. The score and derivative envelopes already imply \(\Omega_j\preceq(KB^2/\varepsilon)I_d\) and \(\|H\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le KD_1\), so no primitive upper matrix bounds are imposed. The proposal-specific envelope \(e_T=T^{-1/2}+r_T+\delta_T\) combines sampling, attraction, and approximation errors. A preliminary moment-norm minimizer localizes a compact empirical-root set; martingale concentration and a quantitative inverse-function argument make the exact-root selector active with probability tending uniformly to one. Stable martingale convergence supplies the mixture, event-truncated realized QV supplies the feasible pivot, finite normal-mixture identification plus polarization supplies the two necessity results, and a bounded in-class law certifies strict logical separation of the directional and matrix frontiers.

related_work: Guo and Xu, Theorems 3.2--3.3, prove marginal and joint IPW-Z Gaussian limits after scaled inverse propensities stabilize; their Section 3.1 no-intercept clipped-LinUCB example supplies numerical evidence of two modes, not a proved finite-attractor theorem or certification of the present class. Guo--Xu is an informed-by comparator. Saco, Theorem 5.14 and Design A in Section 6.6, establishes a pointwise realized-QV pivot under variance growth and illustrates random post-burn-in variance; Theorem 2 is the sole direct strict tightening, giving uniform validity over the conditional finite-attractor class and deriving truncation inactivity from common basin-covariance, attraction, and exact-root localization controls. The Abstract and Introduction of Shen and coauthors distinguish directional stability from full-matrix stability; that distinction informs Theorems 3--4, while the finite-basin every-level converses and bounded separation witness are not presented as a strict comparator chain. Han studies an orthogonal instability mechanism and target: for generalized Gaussian Thompson sampling, Proposition 2.6 and Theorem 2.7 on PDF pages 9--10, together with introduction equation (1.4) on page 4, identify the joint optimal-arm pull-proportion and noise limit with the unique invariant law of a continuous-state SDE. Han's Theorem 3.2 on PDF page 12 and introduction equation (1.5) on page 5 give Gaussian normalized-mean limits for stable arms and an SDE-defined semi-universal limit for multiple optimal arms; the body reports simulation evidence that the latter law is genuinely non-Gaussian, and Corollary 3.3 on PDF page 13 constructs confidence intervals from its quantiles. Han is close motivation, not a result anticipating Theorems 1--4 or the bounded Guo--Xu certification question. Leiner, Dunn, and Ramdas study off-policy M-estimation under working-model misspecification for adaptively collected bandit data. Their target is a projected solution under a stationary evaluation policy, and flexible variance stabilization permits unstable or nonconvergent logging policies; this is an informed-by comparator rather than a same-path-QV or finite-attractor result. Borkar supplies local lock-in bounds, and Pemantle supplies unstable-point avoidance, but neither certifies the bounded recursion. Aldous and Eagleson supply stable-convergence language. Mourrat supplies only the bounded-martingale central-limit and quadratic-variation ingredient. Teicher together with Andrews and Mallows supplies identification of centered normal scale mixtures. Qian and coauthors and Liao and coauthors define the HeartSteps causal-excursion consumer. Zhang, Janson, and Murphy study pooled longitudinal adaptive sampling with Z-estimation and an adaptive sandwich estimator in a fixed-within-user, growing-participant regime. Thus the comparison supports a field-tier conditional theorem bundle, with Saco as its only strict-tightening comparator and no second strict frontier.
technical_internal_limitation: The two slopes do not form a Markov state because clipped-UCB decisions also depend on the inverse ridge Gram coordinates. The open-ended question therefore concerns the slope projection of the augmented chain \(Z^{\mathrm{GX}}_t\) on \(\mathsf E_{\mathrm{GX}}\); \(\mathsf K_{\mathrm{GX}}\) indexes only its initial slopes and is not an invariant chain state space. This bounded Rademacher recursion is not yet shown to have finite projected tail selection, a relative-basin-interior Cesaro attraction modulus, or any separately specified causal-score structure, so it is not claimed to belong to \(\mathfrak P_T\) and Theorems 1--2 are not claimed to apply. Optional Gaussian moment-extension subquestion: after the bounded-model dynamics are classified, determine whether the published Gaussian-noise recursion admits analogous dynamics under suitable moment controls. This optional subquestion is not a premise, deliverable, theorem, or part of the bounded-model open-ended question. Correct coverage at one isolated nominal level also does not identify the scale mixture: two unequal basin variances can be paired with a deterministic scale whose symmetric interval has the desired probability at that one level. Theorem 3 deliberately requires every nominal level.
honest_scope: The project establishes a field-tier inference frontier conditional on membership in the common-envelope finite-attractor class. Saco is the only direct strict-tightening comparator; the absence of a second direct strict frontier caps the contribution at field tier, which is the requested floor and achieved target. Guo--Xu, Shen and coauthors, Han, Leiner--Dunn--Ramdas, Borkar, and the remaining cited papers serve as informed-by comparators, ingredients, close motivation, or orthogonal regimes. The project treats a growing-horizon superpopulation adaptive experiment with a known randomization rule, not a pure fixed-finite-population randomization theorem. The bounded two-basin construction is solely an elementary, non-novel existence witness for strict logical separation between contrastwise and matrixwise invariance. It is not evidence that either the specified bounded Rademacher analogue or the published Gaussian no-intercept Guo--Xu recursion satisfies the finite-attractor, attraction, or common-envelope conditions. The open-ended question concerns only the slope-projected dynamics of the augmented bounded chain and does not assert membership in \(\mathfrak P_T\) or applicability of Theorems 1--2. Any future inference theorem must separately specify its causal score, parameter space, unique target root, nonzero target contrast, induced scalar target, and every class assumption. The Gaussian moment extension remains optional and open. When \(m=1\), \(J=1\), \(V_J=V_1\) is deterministic, Theorem 1 is ordinary asymptotic normality, Theorem 2 is ordinary realized-QV studentization, and Theorems 3--4 allow \(\Sigma=V_1\).
